articles.title: Guilty of journalism
articles.content: AS a journalist making a living solely in the industry, the challenging times confronting the profession are rarely far from one’s mind. Navel-gazing has become more than a side distraction in some ways. No wonder then that a new book on the industry by a stalwart, Mazhar Abbas, was on the must-read list. He has been active in both journalism and the trade union politics of media organisations; Abbas is someone who many in my generation look up to for being among the few who have been able to do both journalism and its politics proficiently and with integrity. None of this is insignificant. Since the proliferation of electronic media, union politics has rarely attracted journalists of stature. It is worth asking at this stage whether he is one of the last Mohicans. His latest book, Media Under the Shadow of Death, covers a wide range of issues — from the origins of the unions formed in the early years of a fledgling country to issues the industry grapples with today: censorship, violence against journalists, and the challenges of technology. For someone like myself who isn’t very well-versed in the history of union politics, the historical account in the early chapters of the book is a fascinating description of how the Sindh Union of Journalists and the Pakistan Federal Union of Journalists (PFUJ) came into being, and how journalists pushed back against the earlier undemocratic efforts of the state of Pakistan. Beyond the events themselves, discussions with people such as Roedad Khan also offer insight into the ruling elite’s thinking at the time and their attitudes towards democracy and press freedom. At the same time, this earlier period also reveals how far back some unfortunate trends go. Even then, journalists’ biases against one another, or in favour of one political stakeholder over another, allowed the state or government to take advantage. The principles of democracy or freedom of expression never proved bigger than personal likes or dislikes. He, too, quotes the famous story of journalists who went to Gen Ziaul Haq and asked him to delay the elections for fear of a PPP victory. In recent times, one has seen media groups attack each other at the behest of the powers that be. The second pattern, which seems to date back further than we realise, is the inability of media owners to match journalists in opposing the state’s suppressive methods; the latter’s decision to sign a code of conduct during theemergencyimposed by Gen Pervez Musharraf is a case in point. But there are no sweeping judgements, as the financial pressures on the media owners and their limitations are also understood by the author. ‘Media Under the Shadow of Death’ documents the key challenges in Pakistani journalism. The strongest part is perhaps the account of the media under Musharraf. This is partly because it’s a recent period when Pakistan’s media flourished and expanded but also faced challenges, including increased violence against journalists as well as events such as the emergency. The latter happened when the author himself was an elected official of the PFUJ and was organising protests against the dictator’s actions. For those of us who were present at the time — in the trenches or on the sidelines — those were heady times. It seemed then that the political parties, lawyers’ organisations, journalists, and others could push back against a military dictator struggling to sustain his rule. No one thought this was simply a transitory moment; it seemed like a permanent change — though we have grown wiser since. But back then, it was a moment of great hope, and the PFUJ’s role was significant. Even now, reading about it brings a sense of satisfaction. As the author himself notes, it was perhaps the last time the federation acted with unity. However, he doesn’t go into the details of what happened later, or how the organisation not only split but has also become a shadow of its former self since then. With his intimate knowledge of union issues, Abbas could have provided an insight into the present mess in journalistic organisations and perhaps kick-started a debate on possible solutions. This omission is disappointing in some ways. The second strongest part of the book is the section where he discusses the killings of journalists, though given the number of case studies, not each case is tackled with an even hand. Some are detailed and some sketchy. However, the more high-profile the case, the more interesting the details — though they still leave one wanting more. This is especially true of cases such asWali Babar’s, where Abbas provides the details of the deaths that followed the investigations of the journalist’s murder — police officers investigating the case, the prosecutor, and even witnesses were killed as the matter progressed. Similarly, the book details high-profile cases (Hayatullah Khan, Musa Khankhel, Arshad Sharif) as well as low-profile ones that may not have garnered much attention. Overall, the book is a resource compendium rather than a chronological or analytical account. There are historical accounts — a chapter on press laws and then one on the case studies of journalists’ killings. This also means the book’s tone is a wee uneven. Perhaps, as the author says at the outset, the book kept getting delayed because of the fast-changing events in the industry and the polity. This might also explain why the writing and editing needed a bit more work. One can only hope some of these issues are addressed in a second edition if there is to be one — for the information in the book is valuable and deserves to be read by those who still haven’t fallen out of love with this profession despite the filth we wallow in these days.
articles.author: Arifa Noor

articles.title: Is Rahul Gandhi ambitious?
articles.content: MILLIONS of Indians evidently see Rahul Gandhi as their candidate to steer the country out of its deep mess driven by hate-filled divisive politics and a K-shaped economic trajectory plying unprecedented inequality. That seemed to be the unspoken sentiment, if not consensus, at the massive Sundayrally of opposition partiesin Delhi against vote theft. The issue has brought out angry youth on the streets. Rigging of polls betrays, however, an inability to secure popular support through clean elections, which is a blessing. India is not alone in subverting democracy. Narendra Modi’s ride-or-die friendship with Benjamin Netanyahu reveals a shared scorn for secular democracy and minority rights. Netanyahu hopes to disenfranchise Palestinian MPs (strategically called Arabs by a clever political fiat) even as they mock him in turn by holding the balance of power, principally against him, after last week’s elections. Likewise with Modi, whosecontroversial victories in Biharand West Bengal recently benefited enormously as his handpicked election commission disenfranchised millions of Muslim voters and other potential opponents of the regime. Netanyahu rewarded Modi’s friendship by giving his government the Pegasus spyware among other contraptions to undermine democracy. One would readily go along with the view that Gandhi makes for a great candidate to don the mantle of prime minister and also restore its prestige. He has displayed the drive to nurse Indian democracy back to health. But is he as equipped as, say, streetfighters like Priyank Kharge or M.K. Stalin or Akhilesh Yadav to deal frontally with the push which will inevitably arrive in the process of dismantling entrenched fascism? That Sonia Gandhi and both her children — Rahul as the leader of the opposition in the Lok Sabha, Priyanka Gandhi as an outspoken and gritty parliamentarian — called out Israel’s genocide in Gaza, while major parties other than the left looked away is cause to celebrate the family — and also something to worry about as it puts them in the crosshairs of many a foreign and domestic interloper. The fact that the RSS chief hosted an Israeli diplomat as chief guest at the Hindutva body’s annual day on Dussehra is troubling. Has anyone bothered to ask Rahul Gandhi if he was himself interested in the job that so many appear keen to award him? A pivotal question needs to be flagged here about widespread faux expertise over a future prime minister from the opposition. Has anyone bothered to ask Rahul Gandhi if he was himself interested in the job that so many appear keen to award him? A fair guess based on history and Nehru-Gandhi genealogy is that Rahul Gandhi harbours no such ambitions. We could perhaps glean the truth of this hunch from Sonia Gandhi’s soon-to-be released memoirs. The BJP routinely accuses Jawaharlal Nehru and his daughter of political ambition. No Indian prime minister with a clear majority in parliament has offered to resign other than Nehru. In February 1950, Nehru offered to resign as prime minister over the refugee crisis after Partition. Sardar Patel persuaded him to withdraw the offer. Again, in 1958, Nehru announced his desire to step down and take a break from office, citing severe mental fatigue, fading idealism, and deteriorating public standards in Indian politics. A public outcry broke out, and the Congress begged him to stay on. Did Nehru want his daughter to succeed him? On the contrary, there’s plenty of evidence that he desired young socialist leader Jai Prakash Narayan as his deputy in 1952, which JP refused. There was not even a remote hint that he wanted his daughter in his cabinet or to succeed him. Nehru was wary of Morarji Desai from the right-wing of the party. He engineered a plan for senior cabinet ministers to resign to work at the grassroots with the party. He inducted Lal Bahadur Shastri as a minister without portfolio in the prime minister’s office, a clear signal who he was tapping as successor. Shastri’s demise in Tashkent set off another round of worry about Desai manoeuvring. Powerful regional satraps countered the move and promoted Indira Gandhi believing she could be manipulated. Mrs Gandhi favoured supporting Gulzari Lal Nanda. The ‘Syndicate’ supporting her was essentially conservative, pro-business, and staunchly anti-socialist. Mrs Gandhi turned the tables on them in 1969 by staging a split with the support of the communist bloc. When the left abandoned her after the emergency — one of their defining errors — she was swamped by the conservatives including religious revivalists who were largely seen as devising her fateful Punjab policy that would eventually lay her low. Rajiv Gandhi was a scrupulously private family man until Sanjay Gandhi’s death in a plane crash required him to stand with his mother. Her assassination set him up as prime minister. There’s no dearth of recorded evidence of Sonia Gandhi opposing his entry into politics. In an emotional showdown, she forbade him from becoming prime minister, presciently fearing he, too, would be killed. Rajiv’s response was: “I am her son … if I don’t do it, who will?” Ambition? Did Sonia Gandhi try to be prime minister in 1999 when she met the president with a list of 272 supporters? The world knows that she backed Manmohan Singh as prime minister in 2004. But a 2014 book by R.D. Pradhan, a civil servant close to Rajiv and Sonia Gandhi, described how Sonia Gandhi had Manmohan Singh in mind as early as 1999. On her part, Sonia Gandhi did one better. She set up a very effective advisory council to informally but crucially advise the Singh government on progressive issues ranging from poverty alleviation, right to information, right to education, halting disinvestment in public sector undertakings — everything that Nehru and Indira Gandhi would approve of. Rahul Gandhi would in all likelihood follow the precepts. His politically correct upbringing could struggle against the ugliness of right-wing politics that prompted Nehru to offer to resign. There are many more roughly hewn leaders in the progressive pack to confront an ugly pushback that would come from a cornered fascist order. The writer is Dawn’s correspondent in Delhi.
articles.author: Jawed Naqvi

articles.title: Storage deficit
articles.content: THE Strait of Hormuz closed on Feb 28, 2026. Within days, QatarEnergydeclared force majeure. Pakistan, which sourced almost all its LNG from Qatar, asked Saudi Arabia to reroute crude through the Red Sea and released gas it had been holding back for weeks. There was no gas storage and very little oil storage to fall back on, because none had ever been built. The timing made it worse. Years earlier, Pakistan signed long-term LNG contracts. Then IMF-driven tariff changes made gas too expensive for industries running captive power plants, and they switched to solar. Demand fell just as the country was locked into more gas than it needed. The pipelines reached the capacity threshold and the authorities curtailed up to 350 mmcfd of domestic gas. Then the strait closed, Qatari cargoes were stranded, and the curtailed fields had to be switched back on within weeks. Too much gas, then too little, and no storage to manage either. This is not a new problem. Policymakers have known for decades that Pakistan needs oil and gas storage, but have done little about it. Gas storage works by pumping surplus gas into depleted reservoirs when demand is low and drawing it back out when supply runs short. As early as 2004, an ADB study examined 107 locations and recommended two depleted fields in Badin, and a 2022 study added a third. Exploration companies operate these fields and could convert them, but no commercial model has been settled. A guaranteed return for investors, the model that inflated power costs for two decades, would be a mistake. It paid for capacity whether used or not, and gave sponsors little reason to control costs. Competitive bidding works the other way: developers compete on the fee they charge to store and return gas, overrun risk stays with them, and the state only sets the terms. Feasibility tenders were issued in 2024 and again in 2026, a month before the strait closed. Even then, the first facility will cover only 11 to 12 days of consumption, against the month officials say is needed. Oil storage has failed for its own reasons. The main one is that no one is paid to hold it. Marketing companies must keep 20 days of cover, but prices are revised every fortnight, so extra stock risks a loss whenever prices fall, and the pricing formula does not recover the cost of tanks. Most companies stay near the minimum, and the state has never built a strategic reserve of its own. The idea of letting foreign suppliers hold fuel in Pakistan was first floated in 2015. In 2023, the government approved it: suppliers could keep product in bonded storage without paying duty, pay only when they sold locally, and re-export freely. Not one supplier has used it — for three reasons. First, the rules require a foreign supplier to register a presence in Pakistan. Large traders are used to storing oil in places like Fujairah in the UAE or Singapore without opening an office there. Asking them to do so here adds cost and paperwork for little benefit. Second, nothing guarantees a supplier can take its oil back out. A future government facing a shortage could block exports, just when it would want to sell elsewhere. Third, five bodies have a say: customs, the regulator, the State Bank, and the commerce and petroleum ministries. Each writes its own rules, and no one makes them fit together. The current government hasreopened the policy, an admission that it has attracted no investment. The strait showed that fuel stored in the Gulf can be cut off without warning. Fuel held in Pakistan by foreign suppliers, available for local sale, would give the country a cushion next time. The fix requires detail, not reinvention. The rules must state who can take part without a Pakistani company, how ownership changes when part of a tank is sold, how banks process those sales, and which single office settles disputes. Traders choose where to store oil based on how fast licences come and whether rules stay stable. Fujairah attracts traders not because its government built the tanks, but because it made storage simple and predictable. In both cases, the government need not spend its own money. Its job is to write clear rules, issue licences quickly, and honour its commitments. Pakistan has paid for the lack of storage twice this year, first with more gas than it could use, then with too little. The gas sites were identified over 20 years ago; the oil policy has existed for years. What has been missing is the will to follow through. Hormuz will not be the last disruption, and if storage is not ready before the next one, the cost will again fall on industry, on households, and on a treasury paying premium prices for emergency cargoes. The next closure will not wait for another feasibility study. The writer is a corporate lawyer working in the energy and infrastructure sector across the Middle East and Pakistan.
articles.author: Srraa Tahir

articles.title: Facing menopause
articles.content: MENOPAUSE. It’s part of life, part of ageing, part of being a woman. All true. The best option for women is to keep a ‘this too shall pass’ or something similar to a ‘close your eyes and think of England’ kind of attitude while going through it. Not true. Nor wise. Or fair. American actor Halle Berry’s famous words in a press conference in 2024 outside the Capitol Hill building, “I am in menopause, OK?” got the world’s attention. In the medical world, menopause has always just been a side note. Women have learnt to bear it; doctors are trained to ignore it. So let’s look at some facts. Whether it is peri- or post-menopause, brought on naturally with the passage of time, or suddenly due to medical interventions, it is a monumental biological transition. One of the many vital systems in the body is shutting down. The system shutting down is, of course, the reproductive system, the one responsible for producing extremely vital hormones since birth, and this next part should be in all caps, directly related to not just reproduction but brain, heart, bone, and musculoskeletal health among others. How can this profound event not affect the mind and body? Two hormones — oestrogen and progesterone — are depleted as women enter menopause. Let’s only discuss oestrogen for now, as it is the more vital of the two. And let’s start with one aspect of its role: oestrogen and the brain. Simply put, oestrogen or more accurately, estradiol, gives energy to the brain. When oestrogen is depleted, brain energy is depleted. According to research, by the time women reach post-menopause, almost 30 per cent of their brain energy has been depleted. Neurons slow down, potentially leading to brain fog, poor memory, word retrieval problems, low mood/ depression, heightened anxiety, and panic attacks, among other debilitating symptoms. Women have learnt to bear it; doctors are trained to ignore it. It’s a neuro-endocrine event in its full glory. And before one attributes some of these symptoms to the emotions ignited by the depravity of our world leaders these days — a valid reason indeed for the frequent bouts of grief and bewilderment experienced by many regardless of gender — let’s take a moment to understand menopause as well, in the hope of bringing relief to some of us at least. Unhelpfully, menopause does not follow a rigid timeline or fixed symptoms. It can manifest as anything from exhaustion, musculoskeletal pain, and poor sleep — which has its own serious repercussions — to widely experienced symptoms like hot flashes and night sweats. It can also cause metabolic changes and fat redistribution, urinary symptoms, painful intercourse, and an increased risk of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease. Symptoms can sometimes be uncommon — like painfully itchy ears — or silent — like severe bone loss that leads to osteoporosis if not caught early. The list is as endless as is the correct diagnosis, while help remains elusive. Of course, one must keep an eye on the usual suspects: lifestyle, diet, exercise, sleep, hydration — and stress, which deserves a special mention for making matters more muddled and insidious. Cortisol, a hormone the body produces during stressful events, exists in direct and opposite balance to the production of oestrogen. Cortisol increases, oestrogen decreases. Cortisol decreases, oestrogen increases. In menopause, oestrogen is dropping, and if, at this point, prolonged and escalating stress is thrown into the mix, it can lead to a perfect storm. Oestrogen is in free fall. The effect is neither minor nor fleeting. So how to manage this? Is HRT (hormone replacement therapy), also called MHT (menopause hormone therapy), advisable and/ or available? Have they developed better solutions than what were available a few decades ago? Is breast cancer still associated with HRT? How can women protect their bones during this time? What about their cardiovascular health? Their brain health? These are the questions women should be asking their doctors. Shouldn’t menopause be at the centre of the overall clinical context, instead of each symptom being treated separately? Doctors, too, need to arm themselves with the latest research instead of shooting in the dark — as in the case of Halle Berry, who was misdiagnosed with an STD when the real cause was menopause — or simply placating their patients. Yet, if we are sceptical of the old saying that every dark cloud has a silver lining, it has come true here: Halle Berry’s misdiagnosis led her to push for more federal funding for research and education on menopause, beginning with destigmatising public discussions on the topic. This was truly an excellent use of the platform available to her. Over to our Pakistani celebrities. Women need a voice. A voice that is heard.
articles.author: Nabila Shahjahan Jafar

articles.title: An opening
articles.content: AS the threat of renewed US-Israeli strikes on Iran lingers, a parallel diplomatic process — facilitated by Qatar and Pakistan — is attempting to avert a devastating return to hostilities. Iranian negotiators were in Doha on Sunday to take part in indirect talks aimed at working out a deal, even as speculation of fresh attacks on Iran, following today’s midterm polls in America, continued. US President Donald Trump has not helped matters by toying with the idea of new attacks. The ice was broken late last month when US Vice-President J.D. Vancewrote a letterto Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei. Mr Vance reportedly prefers a diplomatic solution. Earlier, he had led his country’s delegation duringApril’s historic talksin Islamabad. The letter has been well received in Tehran, with Gen Rezaei calling its tone “positive”. Writing to the Iranian security chief was an intelligent move and has begun to show results. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has said that if the US meets his country’s demands, the Strait of Hormuzcould be reopenedwithin two days. That outcome would be welcomed not only by the Gulf states and other regional countries but also by the international community at large, as states across the world have felt the impact of the strait’s closure and the attendant restrictions on trade and oil and gas flows. Mr Vance’s letter has reportedly asked for guarantees regarding Iran’s nuclear programme. On its part, Tehran wants an end to both the sanctions and the US blockade, as well as other concessions from America. Both sides must show flexibility if this push for peace is to succeed. Though the diplomatic progress is welcome, the process could be torpedoed if the US and Israel go ahead with their attack plans. Media reports indicate that Washington and Tel Aviv are prepared to resume hostilities after the midterms. However, US Democratic Senator Chris Murphy, who has been briefed on the plans, has described the latter as “insane” and likely to cause a “devastating escalation”. The Iranian Supreme Leader, on the other hand, has ordered his forces to retaliate to any attack “without geographical restriction”. It would be very irresponsible of the US and Israel to scuttle peace efforts and spark a potentially massive conflict. The regional states do not want war as they are aware of the destruction it will bring. It is time for more mature officials within the US administration, such as Mr Vance, to take the lead in ensuring that the peace process continues unimpeded, while warmongers in America and Israel must be isolated. If this brief opportunity for peace is wasted, sparking a wider conflict, the blame will rest squarely with the US president and the bloodthirsty Zionist regime.

articles.title: Pakistan’s G-24 role
articles.content: PAKISTAN’S new role as chair of G-24 comes at a crucial moment for the Global South. Developing nations are struggling to navigate an era defined by steep tariffs, a revival of industrial policy, weakening multilateralism, rising interest rates, escalating inflation, climate shocks, and global conflicts that have shaken the world economy. And yet, its new position offers Islamabad an opportunity to articulate the concerns of developing economies, build consensus on a common development agenda, and push for a more equitable global financial and economic order. It is a mandate to lead the developing world effectively and to work closely with major powers on critical reforms across international financial institutions. Achieving this will not be easy. For decades, the global financial framework — dominated by the Bretton Woods institutions — has largely served Western economies, while developing nations are asked to shoulder the costs of global macroeconomic volatility while facing disproportionately higher borrowing costs and severe capital constraints. By stepping into its new role, Islamabad assumes the responsibility of presenting these shared grievances as a cohesive agenda for structural change. Central to this effort is redefining how Western economic powers view the developing world. The focus must shift from seeing developing nations as vulnerable economies in need of more debt or debt relief to recognising their contributions to global economic growth. As the finance minister highlighted, the focus must shift to the “immense potential of emerging and developing nations as drivers of investment, innovation, entrepreneurship, and global growth”. Achieving reform will require bridging the gap between rhetoric and policy action. Key priorities for the G-24 mandate must include advocacy for expanded and easier access to concessional financing, an end to tariff-led industrial policies, the revival of multilateralism, and streamlined mechanisms for debt reduction. The traditional economic narrative that places Western financial centres at the core while relegating developing markets to the periphery is no longer sustainable in an interconnected world economy. As the finance minister has noted, the future of developing economies is central to the future of the global economy. While sweeping changes are unlikely to materialise entirely during Pakistan’s tenure, Islamabad has a crucial window to push this debate to the centre of the global reform agenda.
articles.author: Editorial
